title: Homemade Eggnog EVERYONE's Grandma Made (Why Yours Is RUNNY)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, the first time I tasted real homemade eggnog, I was six years old, at Grandma Pearl's farm on Christmas Eve, nineteen fifty. She ladled it out of a big glass punch bowl into little cups, thick and cold and creamy, with nutmeg on top. Mine had no whiskey in it. My father's had plenty. He sang Jingle Bells all the way home in the snow.
scenes.caption: PLENTY OF WHISKEY

scenes.text: Today most people only know the carton from the store, which is thin and sweet and tastes like melted ice cream. And when they make it at home, it comes out runny, or it curdles into scrambled eggs. So tonight I'm giving you Grandma Pearl's eggnog, every step, and the five mistakes that ruin it. And stay with me, because the last secret is the one that makes it thick, and it takes nothing but time.
scenes.caption: THIN AND SWEET

scenes.text: Eggnog is older than the country, honey. In England, rich people drank a hot milk and egg drink with wine or sherry in winter. When it came to the American colonies, people made it with rum, because rum was cheap here, and later with whiskey and brandy. George Washington had his own recipe, and they say it was so strong only the brave would try it.
scenes.caption: ONLY THE BRAVE

scenes.text: On the farm, Grandma Pearl made it with eggs from her own hens and milk and cream from her own cow, still warm. Nothing in it came from a store except the sugar, the nutmeg and my grandfather's bottle. She made it in the morning and set it in the cold springhouse all day to chill. By evening, it was thick enough to stand a spoon in.
scenes.caption: THICK ENOUGH FOR A SPOON

scenes.text: In the old days, people made eggnog with raw eggs. Today, we cook it gently into a custard first, so it's safe for everybody, the children and the grandparents and anybody expecting a baby. And honestly, it tastes better cooked. In a minute I'll show you how, and the trick that keeps it from turning into scrambled eggs.
scenes.caption: COOK IT GENTLY

scenes.text: In our house on Elm Street, eggnog was only for two nights a year, Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve. My mother made it in her big yellow mixing bowl and kept it on the back porch, because the icebox was full of ham. One year the dog got to it first. He spent Christmas Day sleeping under the kitchen table, very happy, and very full.
scenes.caption: THE DOG GOT TO IT

scenes.text: Here's what you need for about six cups. Six egg yolks. Half a cup of sugar. Two cups of whole milk. One cup of heavy cream. A pinch of salt. One teaspoon of vanilla. Half a teaspoon of freshly grated nutmeg, plus more for the top. And a cinnamon stick. If you want it for grown-ups, half a cup to a cup of bourbon, brandy, or dark rum.
scenes.caption: THE INGREDIENTS

scenes.text: And here's mistake number one. Using skim milk or low fat milk. Eggnog is supposed to be rich, honey. It's a once-a-year treat. Thin milk makes thin, watery eggnog that tastes like nothing. Use whole milk and real heavy cream. If you want it a little lighter, use half and half instead of the cream, but never skim.
scenes.caption: NEVER SKIM

scenes.text: And grate the nutmeg yourself if you can. A whole nutmeg costs about the same as a jar of the ground kind, and it lasts for years. Rub it on a small grater, and the smell fills the whole kitchen. Ground nutmeg from a jar that's been in the cupboard since nineteen ninety tastes like dust. That's mistake number two.
scenes.caption: GRATE IT YOURSELF

scenes.text: Step one. In a bowl, whisk the egg yolks and sugar together for about two minutes, until they turn pale yellow and thick, like a ribbon when you lift the whisk. In a saucepan, warm the milk, the cream, the cinnamon stick, the nutmeg and the salt over medium heat, until it's steaming and little bubbles form around the edge. Don't let it boil.
scenes.caption: PALE YELLOW

scenes.text: Step two, and here's mistake number three. Pouring the hot milk into the eggs all at once. The eggs cook instantly into little scrambled lumps. It's called tempering, honey. Pour the hot milk into the eggs very slowly, just a ladle at a time, while you whisk the whole time with your other hand. Warm the eggs up gently, a little at a time.
scenes.query: ladle hot milk into eggs whisking
scenes.caption: A LADLE AT A TIME

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. When about half the milk is in, pour everything back into the saucepan. Now cook it over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon or a spatula, scraping the bottom and corners, for about five to eight minutes.
scenes.caption: STIR CONSTANTLY

scenes.text: Mistake number four is cooking it too hot or too long. It curdles. You want it to reach one hundred sixty to one hundred seventy degrees on a thermometer, no more. Or use the old test. Dip a spoon in, and run your finger across the back. If the line stays clean and doesn't run back together, it's done. Take it off the heat right away.
scenes.query: finger line custard back of spoon
scenes.caption: THE SPOON TEST

scenes.text: And if it does start to curdle a little, sweetheart, don't panic. Take it off the heat immediately and pour it into a cold bowl. Then whisk it hard, or blend it for a few seconds. Small lumps will smooth right out. Then pour it through a fine strainer into a clean pitcher or bowl. Always strain it anyway. It catches the cinnamon stick and any little bits of cooked egg.
scenes.caption: STRAIN IT

scenes.text: So far, whole milk and cream, fresh nutmeg, pale yolks, temper the eggs slowly, and cook it gently to one sixty, then strain it. Stir in the vanilla. Now the secret I promised, the one that makes it thick. Mistake number five is drinking it right away, warm. Warm eggnog is thin. Cold eggnog is thick and velvety, the way Grandma Pearl's was.
scenes.caption: COLD IS THICK

scenes.text: Cover it, and put it in the icebox for at least four hours, and overnight is even better. The custard thickens as it chills, and the flavors of the nutmeg and vanilla come out. That's Grandma Pearl's springhouse. And if you want it extra light and fluffy, whip a half cup of cream to soft peaks right before serving, and fold it in gently.
scenes.caption: THE SPRINGHOUSE

scenes.text: For the grown-ups, stir in the bourbon, brandy, or rum after it's chilled, a little at a time, and taste it. My father liked bourbon. Grandma Pearl liked a mix of brandy and rum, half and half, and she said it was medicinal. Some people make a big batch with the spirits in it and let it age in the icebox for weeks. That's a little too brave for me, honey.
scenes.caption: IT'S MEDICINAL

scenes.text: And always keep a pitcher without any spirits, for the children and for the drivers. I put a little red ribbon around the handle of the children's pitcher, so nobody mixes them up. Learned that one the hard way in nineteen seventy-three, when my nephew Michael drank two cups of the wrong one and fell asleep under the Christmas tree.
scenes.caption: THE WRONG PITCHER

scenes.text: And save those egg whites, honey. Don't throw them away. Put them in a jar in the icebox, and they keep four days. Use them for a batch of divinity, or meringue cookies, or a white cake. Or whip two of them to soft peaks and fold them into the eggnog right before serving, for a frothy, old-fashioned nog. That's how my grandmother's mother made it, back in the eighteen nineties.
scenes.caption: SAVE THE WHITES

scenes.text: To serve it, pour it into a punch bowl or small glasses, and grate fresh nutmeg over the top. Add a cinnamon stick in each glass for stirring. Or a little dollop of whipped cream. It's rich, sweetheart, so small cups. A big glass of eggnog is like eating a whole pie. Grandma Pearl served it in little glass punch cups no bigger than an egg.
scenes.caption: SMALL CUPS

scenes.text: And it's wonderful in other things, too. A splash in your morning coffee. Use it instead of milk for French toast on Christmas morning. Or in a bread pudding, or a pound cake. My granddaughter makes eggnog pancakes on Christmas morning, and the house smells like nutmeg until noon.
scenes.caption: EGGNOG FRENCH TOAST

scenes.text: Homemade eggnog keeps three days in the icebox, in a covered pitcher. Give it a good stir before serving, because it settles. It doesn't freeze well, honey, because it separates when it thaws. So make only what you'll drink in a few days. That's never a problem in my family. The pitcher is always empty by the second day.
scenes.caption: THREE DAYS

scenes.text: And if somebody can't have dairy, sweetheart, you can make it with oat milk or almond milk and a can of coconut cream instead of the heavy cream. It's not quite the same, but it's thick and sweet and full of nutmeg. My grandson's wife can't have milk, and I make her a little pitcher every year. She says it tastes like Christmas, and that's the whole point.
scenes.caption: IT TASTES LIKE CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: So one more time. Whole milk and cream, never skim. Fresh nutmeg. Whisk the yolks and sugar until pale. Temper the eggs slowly with the hot milk. Cook it gently, stirring, to one sixty, and strain it. Chill it overnight. Spirits for the grown-ups, and a ribbon on the children's pitcher. That's Grandma Pearl's eggnog, thick enough to stand a spoon in.
scenes.caption: THICK ENOUGH FOR A SPOON

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Do you love eggnog, or can't you stand it? I know families are divided. The whole playlist of Grandma's recipes is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: LOVE IT OR HATE IT?
